references.text: Matthew's parallel account: "Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins... But they put new wine into fresh wineskins, and both are preserved." This is the closest parallel to Luke 5:38 in the Gospel of Matthew.
Mark's parallel account: "And no one puts new wine into old wineskins... But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins." Mark tells the same parable that new wine requires fresh wineskins.

Paul writes that "if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, all things have become new." The principle that the new gospel demands renewed life and new forms is reflected in the parable of new wine in fresh wineskins.

Paul urges believers to "put off the old self" and "put on the new self", which theologically corresponds with Jesus' image that new wine (the reality of the new kingdom) must be poured into fresh wineskins (renewed life and mindset).

The Epistle to the Hebrews discusses the new covenant in contrast to the old, stating that the first covenant is obsolete. This illustrates the principle in Jesus' parable: the new wine (the new covenant) requires fresh wineskins (new frameworks), not the old ones.

"Behold, I am making all things new," says the Lord. This eschatological promise of complete renewal is related to Jesus' point in the parable: God's new work does not fit into old forms but requires something entirely new.
